newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf allies end meeting on Qatar-Bahrain dispute.
newsitem.headline: Gulf allies end meeting on Qatar-Bahrain dispute.

text.p: Gulf Arab foreign ministers seeking to settle a border row between Bahrain and Qatar ended talks in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh on Tuesday.
A statement issued after the meeting said they would hold a second round of talks in Riyadh on January 12 after briefing their governments on the outcome of their deliberations.

Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Saud al-Faisal, whose country heads a four-man committee formed by a Gulf Cooperation Council summit in December to mediate in the row casting a shadow over the 16-year-old alliance, said the meeting "was positive".
Asked whether Bahrain and Qatar were closer to finding a solution, he told Saudi state-run television:

"The meeting put forward specific proposals...to prepare the atmosphere between the two countries and come out with a compromise formula to allow friendly and neighbouring states to exert efforts to continue the consultations for their benefit ".
He did not elaborate. But years of Saudi mediation in the decades-old row over the three Gulf islands have failed so far.

The foreign ministers of Qatar and Bahrain, who arrived in Riyadh to join their counterparts from Saudi, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, also held separate talks under Saudi sponsorship, Gulf news agencies reported.
The GCC said in a statement that delegates also discussed a draft memorandum of understanding "on ways to solve any future conflict that might arise among GCC states".
Saudi officials earlier changed the venue of the meeting and banned reporters and cameramen from the heavily guarded gates of the GCC headquarters, where the afternoon talks were held.
"Both foreign ministers presented their capitals' stand on the issue during the afternoon session," one GCC official said.

"The atmosphere between the Qatari and the Bahraini foreign ministers appeared to have improved after their counterparts managed to get them to shake their hands after they refused to do so when they first arrived at the airport this afternoon".
Qatar and Bahrain have been locked for decades in a dispute over a cluster of islands, sandbanks and reefs in the Gulf controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s but also claimed by Qatar.
Qatar has taken the case to the International Court of Justice at The Hague, a move bitterly opposed by Bahrain which insists on an Arab solution.
Ties worsened further after Bahrain accused two Qataris of spying and boycotted the GCC's December summit to protest against Qatar's refusal to withdraw the case from The Hague.
Bahrain last month pardoned the two Qataris after a state security court sentenced them to three years in jail for spying.
Tuesday's talks were the first meeting of the committee.
It was scheduled to hold its first meeting in Cairo last month, but it was later postponed at Saudi request.
